d: About Kalyani, the traveller and traditional Indian art enthusiast behind Miles & Memories, a personal journal of heritage, art and travel.
x: Home / About Hello, I’m Kalyani. I’ve always loved travelling, especially to places that carry stories of the past. Old forts, beautiful temples, painted walls, traditional homes, local markets and handmade crafts have a special place in my heart. I often find myself spending more time admiring a carved doorway or an old painting than taking in the usual tourist attractions. I’m also passionate about traditional Indian art, and many of my travels have become a source of inspiration for my own paintings. Miles & Memories is my little space to document these journeys — the places I visit, the people I meet, the history I discover, and the moments I want to remember. Not every journey is perfect. Some places surprise me, some disappoint me, and some make me wish I could stay a little longer. I want to remember them all. Beyond the usual tourist spots Sometimes, the most memorable part of a journey isn’t the famous monument. It might be a centuries-old painting on a haveli wall, a conversation with a local artist, a beautifully carved wooden door, or a quiet moment beside a lake. These are the details I love discovering. And these are the stories I want to share. More miles. More memories. There are still so many places I want to explore, stories I want to hear, and traditions I want to understand. This journal will grow with every journey. Thank you for being part of it. — Kalyani

t: Amer, the Hill Capital the Kachwahas Left Behind
d: For centuries Amer was the seat of the Kachwaha Rajputs. Their rulers became generals of the Mughal empire, built a palace of mirrors, and then moved down to the plain.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Amer, the Hill Capital the Kachwahas Left Behind Stories Behind the Stones Amer, the Hill Capital the Kachwahas Left Behind For centuries Amer was the seat of the Kachwaha Rajputs. Their rulers became generals of the Mughal empire, built a palace of mirrors, and then moved down to the plain. Amer Jaipur Raja Bharmal Raja Man Singh I Mirza Raja Jai Singh I Sawai Jai Singh II Akbar Forts & Palaces Founders & Dynasties From the road, Amer looks like one building that has been poured over the hill. Its pale walls follow the ridge, its gateways step up the slope, and Maota Lake sits below like a mirror. Above it stands Jaigarh; along the ridge, Nahargarh overlooks Jaipur. Together they tell the story of the Kachwaha Rajputs, who held this valley, made themselves indispensable to the Mughal emperors, built one of Rajasthan's most refined palaces, and finally left it for a new city on the plain. Where and when Amer (also spelled Amber) lies in the hills about 11 kilometres from Jaipur's walled city. Encyclopaedia Britannica says it became the Kachwaha capital in the twelfth century and stayed a political centre for about 600 years. Other accounts place the Kachwaha arrival earlier, and local histories say Meena chiefs held the area before them. The palace you see today mostly dates from the late sixteenth century onwards. In 2013 Amer was inscribed as part of the "Hill Forts of Rajasthan" World Heritage Site, alongside Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron and Jaisalmer. The people Raja Bharmal (also written Bihar Mal) made the decision that shaped everything after him. In 1562 he allied Amer with the young emperor Akbar, and his eldest daughter married Akbar. Raja Man Singh I (1550–1614) is generally described as the son of Bhagwant Das, Bharmal's successor. The Metropolitan Museum of Art's catalogue adds that Bharmal had adopted him. He came to Akbar's court in 1562, became one of the emperor's most trusted generals and was counted among his "nine jewels". He governed Bihar and then Bengal, and died in the Deccan in 1614 while serving Akbar's son Jahangir. Mirza Raja Jai Singh I (1611–1667) was a later descendant of Man Singh (see notes on the exact relationship). He ruled Amer from 1621, received the title "Mirza Raja" from Shah Jahan, and served Aurangzeb as a senior commander. Sawai Jai Singh II (ruled c. 1700–1743) was the ruler who moved the court from Amer to the new city of Jaipur. What happened The 1562 alliance turned Amer's rulers into Mughal nobles. In return for loyalty and military service, they gained rank, wealth and a major role at court. A review of Rima Hooja's biography of Man Singh credits him with dozens of campaigns, from Kabul to Bengal and Odisha. He also commanded the Mughal army against Maharana Pratap of Mewar at the Battle of Haldighati in 1576. Building at Amer followed that wealth. Man Singh's palace is usually dated to the 1590s. Britannica dates the start of the main palace to around 1600. UNESCO singles out the buildings and gardens added by Mirza Raja Jai Singh I as a key seventeenth-century phase in a shared Rajput–Mughal court style. You see it as you climb: the columned Diwan-i-Aam (hall of public audience), then Ganesh Pol, the painted gateway into the private palaces. The Jai Mandir, better known as the Sheesh Mahal, has walls and ceilings set with mirror mosaic and coloured glass, so that one lamp can light up the whole room. Maota Lake below was the palace's water source. Jai Singh I's career shows both the peaks and the risks of Mughal service. In 1665 he besieged Purandar in the Deccan and forced Shivaji to sign the Treaty of Purandar. A campaign against Bijapur then failed. He lost favour and died at Burhanpur in 1667 on his way back to court. Above the palace, Jaigarh guarded the hill. The Ministry of Tourism's site says Sawai Jai Singh II began building it in 1726 as a defensive bastion for Amer, roughly 400 metres higher up. The giant Jaivana cannon there is usually dated to 1720. Other histories say the hilltop was fortified much earlier and that Jai Singh II rebuilt and enlarged it. Then the family left. In the late 1720s Jai Singh II laid out Jaipur on the plain below. Common explanations are that Amer, squeezed between hills, had too little room for a growing population and too little water. In 1734 he completed Nahargarh, on the ridge above the new city, as a retreat that also helped defend it. Britannica dates the transfer of the court to 1728, and other sources give 1727. Legends and debates Shila Devi. The small temple of the goddess Shila Devi stands near Ganesh Pol. According to tradition, the goddess appeared to Man Singh in a dream and told him to recover her image from the sea near Jessore in Bengal (now Bangladesh). A stone slab ( shila ) was found and the image carved from it. A more historical version simply says Man Singh brought the image back from his Bengal campaign, and installed it at Amer around 1604. The dinner story. A popular tale says Maharana Pratap insulted Man Singh by refusing to dine with him, and that this led to Haldighati. Many historians treat it as a later invention, noting that it appears in sources written long after 1576. It is best told as a legend. Who built what? Attributions inside the palace vary. Some sources credit Man Singh with starting the Sheesh Mahal, while others link it mainly to Jai Singh I, with work continuing into the eighteenth century. A Rajasthan Archaeology Department plaque, as reported online, attributes Ganesh Pol to Mirza Raja Jai Singh, but some guides credit Jai Singh II. Even the founding of Jaigarh is dated to the eleventh century by some and to 1726 by others. Wisdom to carry forward Amer is often described in terms of glory, but its real story is about trade-offs. t: Eklingji: The King Behind the Kings of Mewar
d: What if a kingdom believed that its true ruler was not the Maharana on the throne, but Lord Shiva himself? The tradition behind Eklingji Temple.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Eklingji: The King Behind the Kings of Mewar Stories Behind the Stones Eklingji: The King Behind the Kings of Mewar What if a kingdom believed that its true ruler was not the Maharana on the throne, but Lord Shiva himself? The tradition behind Eklingji Temple. Kailashpuri Udaipur Mewar Eklingji (Shiva) Bappa Rawal Harit Rashi Rana Kumbha Rana Raimal Temples & Faith Founders & Dynasties Legends & Folklore What if a kingdom believed that its true ruler was not the Maharana sitting on the throne, but Lord Shiva himself? That is the fascinating tradition behind Eklingji Temple, located in Kailashpuri, near Udaipur. Where and when Kailashpuri lies on the road between Nathdwara and Udaipur, in the hills of the old Mewar heartland. It is close to Nagda, one of the earliest seats of Mewar's Guhila rulers. Eklingji is the family deity of the Mewar royal house. Lonely Planet describes it as "an incarnation of Shiva", and the shrine has been at the centre of the kingdom's religious life for many centuries. Much of what we know about the temple's early story comes from the Ekalinga Mahatmya , a Sanskrit text composed in the fifteenth century under the patronage of Rana Kumbha. It records much older traditions, so its account of the eighth century was written down some seven hundred years after the events it describes. The temple itself has witnessed centuries of history. Its present form reflects later rebuilding and restoration, including work associated with Rana Raimal. At the heart of the shrine is a four-faced image of Shiva carved from black stone. Each face is traditionally associated with a different aspect of the divine. The people The temple is traditionally associated with Bappa Rawal, an eighth-century ruler of Mewar. According to the royal tradition, Bappa Rawal received the blessings of the sage Harit Rashi, who taught him to regard Lord Eklingji as the supreme ruler of Mewar. Later chronicles tell how Bappa grew up in hiding near Nagda, tending cattle, before Harit Rashi initiated him into the worship of Shiva and told him to build the temple. The Ekalinga Mahatmya dates his rule to the early eighth century (it gives 728 CE for his founding of Mewar). The House of Mewar itself counts its custodianship from 734 CE. Many later rulers left their mark on the temple. Hammir Singh, who re-established the family's rule in the fourteenth century, carried out major renovations. Rana Mokal (r. 1421–1433) renovated it again. Rana Kumbha (r. 1433–1468) rebuilt it. Rana Raimal (r. 1473–1509) undertook the last major rebuilding of the complex and installed the present image. What happened From then on, the Maharanas of Mewar considered themselves not the owners of the kingdom, but its Diwans — representatives entrusted with governing on behalf of Lord Shiva. It is an extraordinary idea. A powerful ruler could command armies, build forts and administer a kingdom, yet acknowledge a higher authority. The connection between Eklingji and the rulers of Mewar was not merely ceremonial. It became part of the dynasty's understanding of kingship, duty and legitimacy. Inscriptions show how seriously this was taken. In an inscription of 1460, Rana Kumbha describes himself as the personal servant of Eklingji. The rulers' shared title, Ekling-ka-Diwan , expressed the same idea: the god was sovereign and the ruler was his minister. The temple also suffered in Mewar's wars. Live History India notes that it was damaged by invading armies and rebuilt several times. After an attack in the late fifteenth century by Ghiyath Shah, the sultan of Malwa, Rana Raimal is said to have used the ransom from Ghiyath Shah's capture to pay for rebuilding it. What visitors see today largely dates from that fifteenth-century work. Lonely Planet describes the image at its heart as "a towering four-faced, black-marble image of Eklingji". The tradition is still alive. Lakshyaraj Singh Mewar, a member of the former royal family, told ThePrint that Mewar's rulers "have always been its sewak (caretakers), not its kings", and that the real crown rests with Eklingnath ji. Legends and debates Bappa Rawal's identity. Bappa Rawal is a figure of tradition as much as of history. His name is not in the earliest Guhila inscription (Atpur, 977 CE), and later records list him inconsistently. Some historians think "Bappa Rawal" was a title or nickname, possibly for a ruler known from inscriptions as Kalabhoja. The meeting with Harit Rashi belongs to the dynasty's sacred tradition, not to documented history. The image. Descriptions vary. Some call the image four-faced, while others describe five faces, four looking outwards with a lingam rising between them. Live History India gives the faces as Brahma (west), Vishnu (north), Surya (east) and Rudra, a form of Shiva (south). The title "Maharana". Bappa's own title was Rawal . The title Rana belonged to the Sisodia branch that took power in the fourteenth century, and Maharana is later still. The idea of ruling as Eklingji's minister is very old, but the word "Maharana" fits the later centuries better than Bappa's time. Wisdom to carry forward Power is not the same as ownership. The tradition of Eklingji offers a thought worth carrying beyond the temple: leadership can be understood as a responsibility held in trust, rather than a privilege possessed forever. Standing before a temple so closely connected with Mewar's history, one is reminded that even kings believed they were answerable to something greater than themselves. My connection On Day 9 we left Kumbhalgarh at about 7:30 in the morning. After Shrinathji Temple at Nathdwara, we visited Eklingji Temple, associated with Lord Shiva and the historic rulers of Mewar. As I wrote in my diary, "Eklingji's significance goes beyond its architecture: the deity has traditionally been regarded as the spiritual sovereign of Mewar, with its rulers serving in a custodial role." d: Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur and filled a courtyard beside his palace with stone instruments for reading the sky. Why build an observatory this big?
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / The King Who Built Instruments the Size of Buildings Stories Behind the Stones The King Who Built Instruments the Size of Buildings Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur and filled a courtyard beside his palace with stone instruments for reading the sky. Why build an observatory this big? Jaipur Delhi Ujjain Varanasi Sawai Jai Singh II Muhammad Shah Aurangzeb Vidyadhar Science & Astronomy Founders & Dynasties Walk a few minutes from Jaipur's City Palace and you reach a courtyard that looks at first like a sculpture park: a giant triangular wall with a staircase running up its spine, sunken marble bowls, curving ramps and round towers open to the sky. Nothing here is decorative. Each structure is an instrument, built from stone and masonry, for measuring the movements of the sun, moon and stars. The man behind it, Sawai Jai Singh II, is usually remembered as the founder of Jaipur. But he was also a serious student of astronomy, and the Jantar Mantar is the place where those two sides of him meet. He planned a new capital and, right beside his palace, a place to check the sky against the books. Where and when Jai Singh II ruled the Kachwaha Rajput kingdom of Amber (Amer), which was a feudatory state of the Mughal Empire. Different sources put his birth in 1686 or 1688, and his accession in 1699 or 1700. He reigned until his death in 1743. He kept his influence at court even as Mughal power broke apart after 1707. According to the British Museum, Aurangzeb gave him the title "Sawai", meaning "one and a quarter", after he captured the fort of Vishalgarh from the Marathas in 1701. The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur was built in the first half of the eighteenth century. UNESCO describes it as the most significant, most comprehensive and best preserved of India's historic observatories, with about twenty main fixed instruments. It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2010. The walled city around it was inscribed separately in 2019. The people Sawai Jai Singh II is the central figure. The British Museum describes him as a ruler who was also a mathematician, an astronomer and a town planner. He collected astronomical works from Central Asia and Europe, including those of Ptolemy, Ulugh Beg of Samarkand, John Flamsteed and Philippe de La Hire. Muhammad Shah , the Mughal emperor, backed the observatory project with imperial support. Jai Singh's astronomical tables were named after him. Vidyadhar is named by UNESCO as the architect-planner of Jaipur. He laid the city out on a grid inspired by the prastara plan of the Vastu Shastra, the traditional Hindu treatise on architecture. What happened According to the British Museum, Jai Singh raised a practical problem with the emperor. The astronomical tables then in use gave planetary positions that did not match what was actually seen in the sky, and that affected when Hindu and Muslim religious observances were held. His answer was to observe the sky again, more precisely, using instruments far bigger than usual. A bigger instrument can carry finer scales. With imperial backing he built five observatories, all now called Jantar Mantar: at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. Delhi's is usually dated to 1724 and is generally described as the first. Four of the five still stand. The Mathura observatory has been lost, and one account says it was dismantled in the nineteenth century. Spreading the sites out had a scientific use, because readings taken at several locations could be compared. The sites also carried meaning: Delhi was the imperial seat, Ujjain lay on an old Indian prime meridian and Varanasi was a long-established centre of learning. The Jaipur observatory became the largest. Its best-known instrument is the Vrihat Samrat Yantra, a huge equinoctial sundial about 27 metres tall, with a gnomon (the triangular wall that casts the shadow) set parallel to the Earth's axis. The Jai Prakash Yantra is a pair of sunken hemispherical bowls in which the position of the sun can be read against markings. Meanwhile Jai Singh was building a city. Jaipur was laid out in the late 1720s as a planned capital about 11 kilometres from the old fort-palace at Amer. The observatory sits beside the City Palace, part of the same plan. The observations fed into a set of astronomical tables, the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi , dedicated to the emperor. The British Museum dates its completion to 1728. UNESCO says observations at Jantar Mantar contributed to completing these tables. UNESCO notes the site was temporarily abandoned in the nineteenth century and restored several times since, including under Sawai Ram Singh II (1876) and around 1901. Some plaster and scale markings you see today are renewals. Legends and debates When was it built? Sources do not agree. The Ministry of Tourism's site gives 1728–1734, a BBC Sky at Night article says the site was completed in 1734, one researcher's site gives about 1738, and another popular history gives 1724–1727. UNESCO itself says only "the first half of the eighteenth century". The founding of Jaipur is similarly given as 1726, 1727 or 1728. (start of building versus formal founding); 18 November 1727 is the date most often quoted. "Accurate to two seconds." The Samrat Yantra is very often described as the world's largest sundial, accurate to about two seconds. Its scale is divided finely enough to suggest that. But the sun's shadow has a soft, blurred edge, which (as Wikipedia's article points out) makes such precision hard to achieve in practice. Treat the "two seconds" as a measure of the scale's fineness, not a guarantee. The quarter flag. Tradition holds that, because of the "Sawai" title, Jaipur's rulers flew a full-sized flag and a quarter-sized one. The name. "Jantar Mantar" is generally explained as coming from yantra (instrument) and mantra (here meaning calculation or formula). d: Rana Kumbha's great hill fort sheltered a hidden prince and was the birthplace of a hero. It also witnessed the murder of its own builder.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Kumbhalgarh — The Fort That Kept Mewar Alive Stories Behind the Stones Kumbhalgarh — The Fort That Kept Mewar Alive Rana Kumbha's great hill fort sheltered a hidden prince and was the birthplace of a hero. It also witnessed the murder of its own builder. Kumbhalgarh Mewar Chittorgarh Rana Kumbha Mandan Udai Singh II Maharana Pratap Forts & Palaces Founders & Dynasties From a distance, Kumbhalgarh looks less like a building than a line drawn across the Aravalli hills: wall after wall, rising and dipping with the ridges. It was built in the fifteenth century by Rana Kumbha of Mewar. For the next two hundred years it was the place Mewar's rulers turned to when everything else was in danger. Its history follows the rest of Mewar's history closely. A hidden prince was raised here, and a famous ruler was born here. The king who built it was killed here too. Where and when Kumbhalgarh stands in Rajsamand district, high in the Aravallis at about 1,100 metres. According to UNESCO's advisory body, ICOMOS, it controlled the key crossing between Mewar to the south-east and Marwar to the west. In 2013 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List as one of the six "Hill Forts of Rajasthan", alongside Chittorgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amer and Jaisalmer. Mewar was the kingdom of the Guhila dynasty and later of its Sisodia branch. Early Guhila inscriptions name Nagda and Ahar, both near present-day Udaipur, among their seats. Chittorgarh became the kingdom's great capital. After Delhi Sultanate armies took Chittor in 1303, the Sisodias, led by Hammir Singh, re-established the family's rule in the fourteenth century. Later, under pressure from the Mughals, the capital moved west into the hills, to Udaipur (and to Chavand for a time under Maharana Pratap). Kumbhalgarh was never the official capital. Rajasthan Tourism calls it Mewar's second most important citadel after Chittorgarh, and a refuge for its rulers in times of conflict. The people Rana Kumbha came to the throne in 1433, aged about sixteen, after his father Rana Mokal was killed in a palace conspiracy. He ruled until 1468. Mandan was his chief architect. ICOMOS notes that Kumbhalgarh's design is attributed to him by name, which is rare for buildings of this period. Mandan was also an author and theorist at Kumbha's court, and set out his ideas in a treatise, the Rajavallabha . Udai Singh I (Uda) , Kumbha's son, is the one who killed him. He should not be confused with the later and better-known Udai Singh II, founder of Udaipur. Udai Singh II and Maharana Pratap come later in the fort's story, as a child sheltered here and a son born here. What happened Kumbha's reign was one of the high points of Mewar. He fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat. The Vijay Stambh, the "Tower of Victory" at Chittorgarh, commemorates his victory over Malwa, and Live History India dates it to 1448. He is credited with building or rebuilding a large number of forts across Mewar; one count gives 32. He was also a scholar and musician, to whom works on music and a commentary on the Gita Govinda are attributed. The great Jain temple at nearby Ranakpur was built during his reign, and an inscription of 1439 there names him. Kumbhalgarh was his masterpiece of defence. Sources differ on the dates. ICOMOS says the outer walls were built between 1443 and 1458, over older wall structures. A Kumbhalgarh inscription is cited for 1448 as the year Kumbha ordered the fort's construction, and 1458 is often given as its completion. ICOMOS also notes that the fort was largely built "in a single process", which gives it unusual architectural unity. It lists seven gateways, Hindu and Jain temples, a fifteenth-century dam (the Badva Bund) and a stepwell (the Langan Baori) inside the walls. A palace was added much later by a Maharana named Fateh Singh. In 1468 Kumbha was murdered at Kumbhalgarh, near the Mamadev temple, by his own son Uda. About seventy years later, the fort played its most famous role. When the usurper Banbir seized Chittor in the late 1530s, the infant prince Udai Singh II was smuggled out and brought to Kumbhalgarh. James Tod records that its governor, Asa Shah, a Jain merchant, hid the boy by passing him off as his nephew. Udai Singh was crowned here, and his son Pratap is traditionally said to have been born here in 1540. The fort was not invincible. In 1578, two years after Haldighati, Akbar's general Shahbaz Khan took it after a siege. Mewar later recovered it. Legends and debates How long are the walls? Rajasthan Tourism says "some 36 kms", and that figure is repeated everywhere, sometimes with the claim that this is the world's second-longest wall. UNESCO's own evaluation document gives smaller and inconsistent figures: walls of "20km in length" in one place and a perimeter of "14km" in another. Claims about world rankings are popular rather than official, so treat them with caution. "Never captured"? Guides often say the fort fell only once. ICOMOS says it was "only ever captured once and for a short period", in 1578. Other accounts describe it changing hands more than once in the following years. Protecting goddess. Local belief holds that the goddess Banmata protected the fort from attack. This is a matter of faith rather than history. The rescue of Udai Singh. The story of his nurse, Panna Dhai, who is said to have sacrificed her own son so that he could escape, comes from later chronicles and bardic tradition. It is told in the Udaipur story in this collection. Wisdom to carry forward Kumbha built one of the strongest fortresses in India and was killed inside it by his own son. No wall, however long, protects against what happens within a family or a court. Yet the same fort later did exactly what it was built for. It hid a child until he was safe. d: Mewar's most loved ruler lost his most famous battle, then spent twenty years refusing to give in. His horse Chetak is a different kind of story.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Maharana Pratap and Chetak — The Hero, the Horse and the History Stories Behind the Stones Maharana Pratap and Chetak — The Hero, the Horse and the History Mewar's most loved ruler lost his most famous battle, then spent twenty years refusing to give in. His horse Chetak is a different kind of story. Kumbhalgarh Haldighati Mewar Maharana Pratap Chetak Akbar Man Singh I of Amber Udai Singh II Hakim Khan Sur Founders & Dynasties Legends & Folklore Few people from Rajasthan's past are loved as widely as Maharana Pratap, the sixteenth-century ruler of Mewar who would not submit to the Mughal emperor Akbar. And few animals in Indian history are as famous as Chetak, the horse said to have carried him out of the Battle of Haldighati. The two halves of this story stand on very different ground, though. Pratap's resistance is well documented, in Mughal chronicles as well as in Mewar's own records. Chetak, as we know him today, owes most of his story to later poets and ballad singers. Both are worth knowing. It just helps to know which is which. Where and when Mewar is the hilly region of southern Rajasthan around Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and Udaipur, ruled for centuries by the Sisodia line. By the 1560s many Rajput rulers had allied with the expanding Mughal empire of Akbar. Mewar had not. In February 1568, after a siege of about four months, Akbar captured Chittorgarh, the old capital of Mewar. Pratap's father, Maharana Udai Singh II, had already withdrawn into the hills to the west, where he was developing a new capital at Udaipur. Pratap's birth is usually dated to May 1540 (9 May is the date most often quoted). Encyclopaedia Britannica is more cautious and gives "1545?". Tradition, and Rajasthan Tourism, name Kumbhalgarh Fort as his birthplace. The people Maharana Pratap was the eldest son of Udai Singh II and Jaiwanta Bai. When Udai Singh died in 1572, he had wanted a younger son, Jagmal, to succeed him, but Mewar's nobles placed Pratap on the throne at Gogunda. Jagmal later went over to Akbar. Akbar , the Mughal emperor, first tried diplomacy. Between 1572 and 1573 he sent a series of envoys, among them Jalal Khan, Raja Man Singh of Amber, Raja Bhagwant Das and Todar Mal, to persuade Pratap to accept Mughal overlordship. Pratap refused them all. Man Singh I of Amber , the Kachwaha prince, commanded the Mughal army at Haldighati. So Rajputs fought on both sides of this battle. Pratap's side was not made up of Rajputs alone either. Hakim Khan Sur , an Afghan commander, led his vanguard, and Bhil archers under their chief Punja fought alongside him. So did Ram Shah Tomar, the former ruler of Gwalior. Later, the Jain merchant-minister Bhama Shah is remembered for funding Pratap's continued resistance. What happened In June 1576 the two armies met at the Haldighati pass, about 19 kilometres from the fort of Gogunda, north-west of present-day Udaipur. The battle is usually dated to 18 June. Al-Badauni, a Mughal historian who was there, gives 21 June. Badauni counted about 3,000 Mewar horsemen and some 400 Bhil archers, against roughly 10,000 Mughal troops. Later Mewar traditions gave far larger figures on both sides, which the historian Jadunath Sarkar considered exaggerated. The Mughals won, but, as Britannica puts it, the battle became legendary as a Rajput stand against heavy odds. Pratap escaped into the hills. Tradition holds that a Jhala chieftain put on the royal insignia so that the enemy would chase him instead, and was killed. The Mughals briefly occupied Gogunda. What followed is the real heart of Pratap's reputation. For the next twenty years he fought from the hills, harassing Mughal outposts and urging his people not to cooperate with Akbar's tax collectors. He lost a great deal: Kumbhalgarh itself was taken by Akbar's general Shahbaz Khan in 1578. But from the mid-1580s, while Akbar was occupied in the Punjab, Pratap recovered most of his strongholds. Chittorgarh was never one of them. He held court at Chavand, and died on 19 January 1597. Accounts say his death followed a hunting injury. His son Amar Singh I finally came to terms with Akbar's son, the emperor Jahangir, in 1615. Britannica gives 1614, and sources differ on the year. Legends and debates Chetak. The popular story goes like this. At Haldighati, Chetak reared up against Man Singh's war elephant. Wounded, he then carried Pratap away from the battlefield, leaping a stream or ravine, and died soon afterwards. Historians treat it as legend. A study of Rajasthani horse traditions notes that historical sources do not name the horse Pratap rode, or credit it with any unusual feat. The name "Chetak" first appears in an eighteenth-century ballad, the Khumana Raso . The version most people know was popularised by James Tod's Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan (1829), which drew on that ballad. Sarkar thought the elephant episode as exaggerated as the troop numbers. The legend has its own landmark all the same. The Chetak Smarak at Balicha, near Haldighati, is said to mark the spot where the horse died, and the Archaeological Survey of India protects it as a monument. Other battlefield stories. A popular story says that Pratap's estranged younger brother, Shakti Singh, rode after him, killed his pursuers and gave him a fresh horse when Chetak fell. I could not trace this to a contemporary source, so it belongs with the legends. Who won? In recent years some have argued that Pratap actually won at Haldighati, and in 2017 there were moves in Rajasthan to rewrite school textbooks that way. Historians including Rima Hooja have rejected this reading. The contemporary accounts describe a Mughal victory, but one that failed in its main aim, which was to capture Pratap or force his submission. Wisdom to carry forward Pratap's fame rests on a battle he lost. What earned him his place in Mewar's memory was what he did in the twenty years afterwards: living with loss and keeping going without a decisive

t: Painted Homes for Merchants Who Went Away
d: Shekhawati's merchant families made fortunes in Calcutta and Bombay, then spent them covering their homes back in the desert with gods, elephants and steam trains.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Painted Homes for Merchants Who Went Away Stories Behind the Stones Painted Homes for Merchants Who Went Away Shekhawati's merchant families made fortunes in Calcutta and Bombay, then spent them covering their homes back in the desert with gods, elephants and steam trains. Mandawa Shekhawati Rao Shekha Thakur Nawal Singh Merchants & Trade Art & Craft In a Mandawa courtyard, you can look up and see Krishna on one wall, a row of elephants with their mahouts on another, and, tucked into a border, a steam train puffing across the plaster. The people who paid for these paintings often spent most of their lives hundreds of kilometres away, in the counting houses of Calcutta and Bombay. That is the puzzle at the heart of Shekhawati. In a semi-desert region of small towns in northern Rajasthan, there are hundreds of painted mansions, temples, wells and memorials. Many of them were built by families who had already moved away. Why decorate a home you hardly live in? Where and when Shekhawati covers parts of today's Jhunjhunu, Sikar and Churu districts, an arid region north-west of Jaipur. It takes its name from Rao Shekha , a Kachwaha Rajput chief (a branch of the same clan that ruled Amer) who established his authority there in the mid-fifteenth century. By the 1730s, his descendants, the Shekhawat thakurs , had divided the region into semi-independent estates, each with fortified towns and carefully managed water sources such as stepwells and tanks. UNESCO's tentative-list entry, submitted by India in June 2026, explains what happened next. Between about 1740 and 1800, towns on the caravan routes grew quickly, because the thakurs offered merchants security and tax incentives to settle. Mandawa is one example. Its fort was built by Thakur Nawal Singh, and Outlook Traveller dates it to 1755. Trading families settled in the town around it. The people The merchants were Hindu and Jain trading families. Outside Rajasthan they came to be called Marwaris , a broad label that, as the historian Abhishek Parashar notes, often covers people with no connection to Marwar (Jodhpur) itself. In fact, he writes, most of the leading Marwari entrepreneurs came from Shekhawati. Some of India's best-known business families trace their roots here. The Birlas, for example, came from Pilani in Jhunjhunu district. In Mandawa today, havelis carry the names of families such as the Goenkas, Morarkas and Jhunjhunwalas. The painters, local craftsmen, are mostly unnamed; the havelis carry their patrons' names. What happened In the nineteenth century, overland caravan trade declined as commerce shifted to the British-run ports. Many Shekhawati merchants followed the money to Calcutta, Bombay and other colonial centres. They worked as traders, brokers, bankers and insurers, dealing in cotton, jute and opium. A drought-prone homeland pushed them; railways and credit networks made distant business possible. They did not cut their ties with home. From the mid-nineteenth century until about the 1930s, they sent money back to build in their home towns. UNESCO dates the most intense period of patronage to the 1830s through the early twentieth century, with haveli painting at its peak in the middle and later 1800s. A family that wanted to be recognised as an established seth was expected to build more than a house: a temple, a well, a rest house for travellers and, after a patriarch's death, a domed chhatri in his memory. The havelis were usually arranged around courtyards. The outer one was for business and male visitors, and the inner one for family life. Their walls were painted in fresco buono (pigment on wet lime plaster) and fresco secco (on dry plaster), using mineral and plant colours and, later, imported synthetic pigments. The subjects changed with the times. Earlier paintings are full of gods and goddesses, scenes from the epics, folk tales such as the ballad of Dhola and Maru, and processions of elephants and horses. Later ones show British officers, trains, motorcars, gramophones and hot-air balloons. These were new things the merchants had seen in the cities and wanted on their own walls. Some families commissioned havelis late in the nineteenth century after every member had moved away, so a few grand houses were built but barely lived in. As the community settled permanently in the cities during the twentieth century, the painting tradition faded. By the middle of that century it had largely stopped. Legends and debates Why paint a house you have left? The usual explanation is display, and that is part of it. But writers drawing on scholars such as Anne Hardgrove and Kaiwan Mehta suggest something more. The painted buildings helped make the town a "homeland", a place where a family's standing was publicly recorded, in contrast to the cities where it actually did business. The havelis were as much about belonging as about showing off. Dates and numbers. Figures vary. One magazine estimates about 2,000 frescoed buildings, painted from the seventeenth to the early twentieth century. UNESCO's entry focuses on 14 of roughly 38 historic towns. Sources also disagree on when building started (anything from the mid-eighteenth century to the 1840s), depending on whether they mean forts and early temples or the great wave of merchant havelis. Satire or simply news? The stiff, overdressed Europeans in some later paintings are sometimes read as gentle mockery of the colonial rulers. They may just as well show painters recording something new and strange. There is no written evidence either way. Survival. Nearly all the havelis are privately owned. Some are decaying; a few have been restored as museums or heritage hotels. Wisdom to carry forward These families made their fortunes far away, yet they spent much of it on walls in towns they rarely saw. The paintings were a way of saying "we still belong here". t: A Forest of Marble Pillars: The Making of Ranakpur
d: A merchant's vision, a king's land grant and an architect's genius produced one of India's great Jain temples, hidden in a valley of the Aravallis.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / A Forest of Marble Pillars: The Making of Ranakpur Stories Behind the Stones A Forest of Marble Pillars: The Making of Ranakpur A merchant's vision, a king's land grant and an architect's genius produced one of India's great Jain temples, hidden in a valley of the Aravallis. Ranakpur Pali Mewar Dharna Shah Depaka Rana Kumbha Somasundara Suri Temples & Faith Art & Craft Merchants & Trade You come upon Ranakpur almost by surprise. The road winds through the green folds of the Aravalli hills, and then a great pale temple appears in a quiet valley, its spires and domes climbing up the slope. Inside, the light falls between rows and rows of carved marble pillars, and the building seems to go on and on. This is the Chaturmukha Dharana Vihara, the main Jain temple at Ranakpur. Its name holds two clues to its story: chaturmukha , "four-faced", describes its design, and Dharana recalls the man who paid for it. Behind it stand three people we can actually name from the stone itself: a Jain merchant, an architect, and a king. Where and when Ranakpur lies near the town of Sadri in Pali district, on the western side of the Aravallis, in the old kingdom of Mewar. The temple belongs to the Shvetambara Jain tradition and is dedicated to Adinatha (also called Rishabhanatha), the first of the 24 Tirthankaras, the great teachers of Jainism. It is counted among the most important Jain pilgrimage sites in India. The firmest date we have comes from a Sanskrit inscription of 47 lines carved on a pillar near the entrance. It is dated 1439 CE (Vikram Samvat 1496), in the reign of Rana Kumbha, who ruled Mewar from 1433 to 1468. Work clearly continued for many years after that: sources give different end dates, and Cornell University's architecture collection simply places the building between about 1440 and 1500. The temple is built in the Maru-Gurjara style of western India and is enormous, roughly 60 by 62 metres, about the size of a Gothic cathedral. The people Dharna Shah (also written Dharanaka or Dhanna Shah) was a Jain merchant of the Porwal community. Several accounts describe him as a minister at Rana Kumbha's court. The inscription names him as the builder, the person who commissioned the temple. Depaka (also Depa or Deepaka) is named in the same inscription as the architect. Temple tradition says he came from a nearby village and that his plan won Dharna Shah over after better-known designers had failed. Rana Kumbha was the Sisodia ruler of Mewar, famous for his forts, including nearby Kumbhalgarh. He granted the land, and the town's name, Ranakpur, is generally linked to him. The inscription praises Kumbha and a long line of his predecessors and says the temple was built "by his grace and on his orders", which shows how a Hindu king and a Jain merchant could share credit for a sacred building. Acharya Somasundara Suri , a leading monk of the Tapa Gaccha, is named as the person who consecrated the temple. He is also described as Dharna Shah's spiritual guide. What happened The heart of the design is the chaturmukha , or four-faced, plan. In the central sanctum sits a white marble image of Adinatha with four faces, one looking out of each of four doorways. Each doorway opens onto halls, which open onto further halls, so a worshipper can approach the Tirthankara from any direction. The four faces are usually read as a symbol of the Tirthankara's message reaching all four directions of the world. Around this centre the builders arranged dozens of halls, small domed pavilions and a ring of subsidiary shrines (devakulikas), with five spires rising above. Because the halls are open on so many sides, light and air move through the whole building, and as you walk the view keeps changing between columns. What most visitors remember is the carving. The ceilings are worked into concentric rings and lace-like pendants. Pillars carry dancers, musicians, elephants and lions. One celebrated panel shows Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, sheltered by a serpent with a canopy of many hoods. It is often said to have 1,008 snake heads, carved from a single slab. The temple did not always flourish. Accounts describe a long decline: the surrounding population thinned, and the site was damaged and neglected. In the twentieth century the Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi, the Jain trust that manages it, carried out a major restoration. Sources give different dates for this work, from the early 1900s to a reopening in 1953. Legends and debates The dream. According to tradition, Dharna Shah dreamt of a Nalinigulma vimana , a celestial palace, and wanted the temple to look like it. This is a cherished story, not a documented event. The 1,444 pillars. The number is repeated everywhere, but it is best understood as the traditional figure. Published counts differ widely: one widely used reference gives 1,444, while others list about 420 or 426 columns. It is not clear how the traditional number was reached, for example whether it counts pilasters and small supports. A popular saying adds that the pillars cannot be counted at all. What every source agrees on is that the carving varies from pillar to pillar. The starting date. Some accounts say construction began in 1389. That is hard to fit with the inscription, which credits Rana Kumbha, who did not come to the throne until 1433. The inscription of 1439 is the safest anchor. The unfinished pillar. Tradition holds that one pillar was left deliberately incomplete, or that it fell each night as it was built. This is folklore, often told as a lesson about humility. Wisdom to carry forward At Ranakpur the person whose name matters most, the architect, survives mostly as a single word in an inscription. Thousands of carvers left no names at all. The building reminds us that great works are almost always shared: a merchant's money, a king's land, a monk's blessing, and the patience of many unnamed hands. It is also a lesson in repetition. d: A father's offhand remark, an uncle's promise and a desert called Jangladesh. How a younger Rathore prince built Bikaner, and why its famous fort came a century later.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / A Son’s Kingdom in the Sand — Rao Bika and the Founding of Bikaner Stories Behind the Stones A Son’s Kingdom in the Sand — Rao Bika and the Founding of Bikaner A father's offhand remark, an uncle's promise and a desert called Jangladesh. How a younger Rathore prince built Bikaner, and why its famous fort came a century later. Bikaner Marwar Rao Bika Rao Jodha Rawat Kandhal Karni Mata Raja Rai Singh Karan Chand Founders & Dynasties Forts & Palaces Legends & Folklore Most cities in Rajasthan are named after the person who founded them, but few founding stories begin with a joke. Bikaner's does, at least as it is usually told: a father teases his son in front of the court, and the son takes the teasing as a dare. Within a generation that son had a capital of his own in the northern Thar. The fort visitors queue for today, Junagarh, is not the one that son built. It came about a century later, and keeping those two moments apart is the key to understanding Bikaner. Where and when Bikaner lies in the north of the Thar Desert, in a dry region that older sources call Jangladesh. Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the start of Rao Bika's conquests in the area to about 1465 and says he began building the city in 1488. The name is usually explained as "the settlement of Bika." Bika's family were Rathores, rulers of Marwar to the south-west. His father, Rao Jodha, founded Jodhpur in 1459. Bika did not inherit Jodhpur. Like several of his brothers, he had to win territory for himself. Incredible India, the Government of India's tourism site, notes that Bikaner sat on caravan routes and grew into a trading centre. It also says Bika invited merchants to settle there and gave them land. The people Rao Bika was a son of Rao Jodha , the Rathore ruler who moved his capital from Mandore to Jodhpur. Britannica records Bika's death in 1504. Rawat Kandhal was Bika's uncle, Jodha's brother. He went with Bika on the campaign that created the new state. Karni Mata was a revered holy woman of the Charan community. Bikaner's rulers came to regard her as their patron goddess, and her temple stands at Deshnok, south of the city. Raja Rai Singh ruled Bikaner from 1571. He was one of Emperor Akbar's most distinguished generals and became the first ruler of Bikaner to hold the title raja . His minister Karan Chand oversaw the building of the fort we now call Junagarh. What happened Bikaner's own tradition places the story's turning point in 1465. Bika came late to his father's court and sat whispering with his uncle Kandhal. Jodha remarked that the two must be plotting to conquer new lands. According to the tradition, uncle and nephew took the remark as a challenge and set out to do exactly that. Accounts say Jodha approved, and that Bika left with only a few hundred men. Over the next two decades Bika built up a territory in Jangladesh. He made alliances where he could, including a marriage with the Bhati family of Pugal, and he took advantage of rivalries among the Jat clans who held much of the land. In about 1478 he built a modest stone fort at a site called Rati Ghati. Its remains are said to survive near the Lakshmi Narayan temple in the old city. Britannica gives 1488 as the year he began building the city, and that is the date Bikaner usually celebrates as its founding. When Bika died in 1504, Bikaner was a real but small state. The decisive change came with Rai Singh, who reigned from 1571 until 1611 or 1612 (sources differ). His service as a Mughal general brought the wealth that paid for a far grander fortress. Construction of its walls and moat is generally dated from 1589 to 1594, under the supervision of his minister Karan Chand. The fort was first called Chintamani . It became known as Junagarh, the "old fort", only in the early twentieth century, after the royal family moved to the new Lalgarh Palace. Later rulers added palaces inside it, such as Anup Mahal, Chandra Mahal and the twentieth-century Ganga Mahal. The painted and mirrored interiors built up over many reigns. None of them date from Bika's lifetime. Legends and debates The founding remark. The story of Jodha's teasing comes from Rathore and Bikaner tradition. It is best read as a story the dynasty told about itself, not a verbatim record. Karni Mata's role. According to devotional tradition, Karni Mata blessed Bika, predicted that his fame would surpass his father's, and laid the foundation of his fort at Rati Ghati in 1485. These details show how closely Bikaner's rulers tied their legitimacy to her, but they are matters of faith, not documented history. The name. James Tod, the nineteenth-century British writer, recorded a story that the land belonged to a Jat called Naira (or Nera), who gave it up on condition that his name be joined to Bika's: Bika + Ner = Bikaner. It is a tradition Tod recorded, not a settled etymology. Dates. Sources variously give 1465, 1472, 1478, 1485 and 1488. The safest summary: Bika began carving out his territory from about 1465, and the city is conventionally dated to 1488. "Never conquered." Junagarh is often called a fort that was never taken. Yet the government tourism page for the fort itself mentions that the Mughal prince Kamran Mirza briefly occupied Bikaner's fort in 1534, before Rai Singh's rebuilding. "Rarely taken, and never held for long" is more accurate. Wisdom to carry forward The building Bikaner is famous for was not made by its founder. Bika's own fort is now mostly gone. What he left behind was harder to photograph: a territory, alliances, settled merchants and a dynasty. Without that groundwork, Rai Singh's wealth would have had nothing to build on. In front of a magnificent facade, it is worth asking two questions: who paid for this, and who made it possible to build here at all? The answers are often different people, a century apart. t: The Fort on the Mountain of Birds — Rao Jodha and the Founding of Jodhpur
d: In 1459 a Rathore ruler left his ancestral capital for a bare rock hill. A hermit's curse and one man's sacrifice became part of Mehrangarh's founding story.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / The Fort on the Mountain of Birds — Rao Jodha and the Founding of Jodhpur Stories Behind the Stones The Fort on the Mountain of Birds — Rao Jodha and the Founding of Jodhpur In 1459 a Rathore ruler left his ancestral capital for a bare rock hill. A hermit's curse and one man's sacrifice became part of Mehrangarh's founding story. Jodhpur Marwar Rao Jodha Rao Ranmal Rajiya Bambhi Cheeria Nathji Karni Mata Founders & Dynasties Forts & Palaces Legends & Folklore From almost anywhere in Jodhpur's old city you can look up and see Mehrangarh. Its walls rise straight out of the rock, so it is hard to tell where the hill ends and the fort begins. Rudyard Kipling is often quoted as calling it the work of "angels and giants." It was in fact begun in 1459 by a ruler who had spent years in exile winning back his inheritance, and who wanted a capital harder to take than the old one. Jodhpur's tradition adds two more figures: a hermit who did not want to leave, and a man remembered for giving his life to the foundations. Where and when Jodhpur lies on the eastern edge of the Thar Desert, at the heart of the historic region of Marwar. Before 1459 the Rathore rulers of Marwar governed from Mandore, a few kilometres to the north. The Mehrangarh Museum Trust records that Rao Chunda (r. 1384–1428) acquired Mandore as part of a dowry and made it his capital. Mandore was old and exposed. According to the Trust, Rao Jodha moved "to a new site six miles to the south, on an isolated rock," which offered height and natural defences. The hill rises about 400 feet above the plain (some sources say 410). Tradition calls it Bhaurcheeria, the "mountain of birds." The Trust explains the name Mehrangarh as "fort of the sun," a reference to the Rathores' claimed descent from Surya, the sun god. According to their bards, the clan's ancestors had once ruled Kanauj, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, before moving west to Marwar. The people Rao Jodha ruled Marwar from 1438 to 1489, according to the Mehrangarh Museum Trust. He was a son of Rao Ranmal (also called Ridmal). Rao Ranmal was killed at Chittor in 1438 during a power struggle at the Mewar court. Accounts say Jodha escaped and spent years rebuilding his strength before recovering Mandore, usually dated to 1453. Jodha had many sons. Among them were Satal and Suja , who succeeded him in turn at Jodhpur, and Bika , who founded Bikaner. Cheeria Nathji , the hermit, Rajiya Bambhi , and Karni Mata , the Charan holy woman revered by the Rathores, belong to the founding legends discussed below. What happened Once Jodha had recovered Mandore, he could think about a new capital. Britannica, the Mehrangarh Museum Trust and Incredible India all date Jodhpur's founding to 1459. The foundation of the fort is traditionally placed on 12 May 1459, and Jodhpur still marks that date as its founding day. Jodha's fort was much smaller than the one visitors see today. Mehrangarh grew over the next four centuries. The Trust notes that Rao Maldeo (r. 1531–62) strengthened the gates and walls after the fort was captured by Sher Shah Sur's forces in 1544. Later rulers added palaces and gates. Fateh Pol commemorates a victory over the Mughals in 1707. Jai Pol was built by Maharaja Man Singh in 1806 after his victory over the armies of Jaipur and Bikaner, a reminder that Jodha's descendants in Jodhpur and Bikaner did not always stay friendly. The city of Jodhpur grew in the fort's shadow and took its founder's name. The fort is still in the care of the former royal family. The Mehrangarh Museum Trust names the current head of the clan, Maharaja Gaj Singh II, as custodian of the fort, credited with preserving its buildings and developing its museum. Legends and debates The hermit's curse. According to legend, the hill had one inhabitant, a hermit called Cheeria Nathji, the "lord of birds." When Jodha's men cleared the hill to build, the hermit was forced out. In anger he cursed the place with scarcity of water. One version says Jodha turned to Karni Mata, who persuaded the hermit to leave. Another says the king's men evicted him and the new walls collapsed. In most tellings Jodha tried to appease him by building him a dwelling and a temple within the fort. Rajiya Bambhi. According to tradition, a man named Rajiya Bambhi (also recorded as Rajiya Bhambi and as Rajaram Meghwal) volunteered to be buried alive in the fort's foundations to bring it good fortune. He did so on the condition that the ruling family would look after his descendants. Some retellings say his sacrifice was needed to break the hermit's curse. Others treat the two stories separately. Accounts say his family was granted land in an area of Jodhpur called Raj Bagh, where his descendants still live. A memorial to him has been pointed out to visitors inside the fort. We cannot know what really happened in 1459, but the city has kept his name alive for centuries. Karni Mata's foundation. Devotional accounts of Karni Mata say she laid the foundation of Jodhpur's fort in 1459 and foretold that Jodha's descendants would rule it for many generations. This is a matter of faith. Dates and spellings. Jodha's dates are usually given as 1416–1489, and his accession as 1438 or 1439. The hill appears as Bhaurcheeria, Bhakurcheeria or Chidiya-tunk, and the hermit sometimes as Chidiya Nath. The "angels and giants" quote. It is widely attributed to Kipling, but I could not trace it to a specific published work. Wisdom to carry forward Mehrangarh was built to impress, and it still does. Its own founding legend, though, puts an ordinary man at the bottom of the walls, not a king or a god. Whether or not Rajiya Bambhi was really buried there, Jodhpur chose to remember the bargain: a life given, and a family to be looked after in return. That is worth noticing in a place so full of royal portraits. A city's story is also kept by the people who insist on remembering the names that would otherwise be forgotten. My connec

t: The Fort That Never Emptied — Rawal Jaisal and the Golden City
d: In 1156 a Bhati prince moved his capital to a lonely three-peaked hill. Nearly nine centuries later, people still live inside the fort he founded.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / The Fort That Never Emptied — Rawal Jaisal and the Golden City Stories Behind the Stones The Fort That Never Emptied — Rawal Jaisal and the Golden City In 1156 a Bhati prince moved his capital to a lonely three-peaked hill. Nearly nine centuries later, people still live inside the fort he founded. Jaisalmer Thar Desert Rawal Jaisal Jait Singh II Lunkaran Guman Chand Patwa Diwan Mohata Nathmal Forts & Palaces Founders & Dynasties Merchants & Trade Most of Rajasthan's great forts are now museums. You buy a ticket, walk through empty courtyards and imagine the people who once lived there. Jaisalmer is different. Inside its yellow sandstone walls people still cook, pray, run shops and hang out washing. UNESCO describes it as a township "still inhabited today." The fort is named after the man who chose the hill: Rawal Jaisal, a prince of the Bhati Rajputs. Where and when Jaisalmer stands deep in the Thar Desert, in the far west of Rajasthan. Encyclopaedia Britannica records that the town was founded in 1156 by Rawal Jaisal. The fort sits on Trikuta, a three-peaked ridge of sandstone rising out of the flat land around it. Before Jaisalmer, the Bhatis ruled from Lodurva (also spelled Lodhruva), roughly 15 km away. Accounts say Lodurva had been sacked in the mid-twelfth century, and Jaisal moved the capital to a site that was easier to defend. Britannica describes Jaisalmer as a major caravan centre. Its wealth came largely from levies on camel trains crossing the Thar towards the ports of Gujarat. When sea trade through Bombay grew, the caravans dwindled and Jaisalmer declined. The people Rawal Jaisal was a Bhati Rajput ruler. The Bhatis claim descent from the Yadu clan, the lineage of Krishna, and Jaisalmer's rulers used the title Rawal , later Maharawal . One account says he was passed over for the throne of Lodurva in favour of a younger half-brother, though I could not confirm this from a stronger source. Jait Singh II and his son Lunkaran were sixteenth-century rulers of Jaisalmer, linked to the dam, garden and first cenotaph at Bada Bagh. Guman Chand Patwa (Guman Singh in some sources) was the merchant who began the five mansions of Patwon ki Haveli. Diwan Mohata Nathmal was the state's prime minister. Maharawal Beri Sal commissioned Nathmal ki Haveli as his residence. What happened Jaisal's first fort was reportedly built of mud, and it was rebuilt and enlarged in stone over the following centuries. What survives is a dense hilltop town of palaces, houses, wells and temples, ringed by walls and bastions. Seven Jain temples, built in yellow sandstone between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, stand inside, alongside Hindu temples such as the Laxminath temple. UNESCO highlights this mix, calling Jaisalmer an important example of a fort that is both sacred and urban. Its history was not peaceful. Jaisalmer was besieged by Delhi Sultanate armies, most famously under Alauddin Khalji in the late thirteenth century. Tradition records episodes of jauhar , in which the fort's women chose death by fire rather than capture. Dates and numbers vary between accounts. In the sixteenth century, outside the walls, Jait Singh II built a dam to create a reservoir. His son Lunkaran laid out a garden beside it and raised a memorial chhatri on the hill above. This became Bada Bagh, the "big garden", where later rulers added their own cenotaphs. The last, intended for Maharawal Jawahir Singh, was left unfinished after Indian independence. In the town below, merchants turned profits into stone. Patwon ki Haveli was planned from about 1805 and took decades to finish. Nathmal ki Haveli followed in 1885. The main Patwa mansion, Kothari's Patwa Haveli, is now a museum. In 2013 the World Heritage Committee, meeting in Phnom Penh, inscribed six forts as the Hill Forts of Rajasthan: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber and Jaisalmer. The same decision warned that the hill under Jaisalmer was vulnerable to water seepage and that buildings inside the fort needed better conservation. The people who keep the fort alive also strain it. Legends and debates The sage on Trikuta. According to legend, when Jaisal came to the hill he met a sage, usually named Eesul. The sage told him that Krishna had prophesied a descendant of the Yadu clan would one day found a kingdom here. Tradition also credits the sage with a darker prediction: that the fort would be sacked "two and a half" times. Local storytellers link this to the three jauhar episodes, one of them counted as a "half". These are cherished traditions, not documented events. The 1156 date. Britannica and most official sources give 1156. Surrounding details, such as when Lodurva was sacked, are reported inconsistently (1152 to 1178). How many people live in the fort? Figures range from about 2,000 to about 4,000 depending on the source and year. "A few thousand" is the honest answer. The two brothers of Nathmal ki Haveli. It is said that two brothers, Hathi and Lulu, each built one half of Nathmal ki Haveli. That would explain why the two sides match overall but differ in detail. The government tourism site presents this as legend, and so should we. Sonar Kella. The nickname "Golden Fort" comes from the colour of the stone. It became famous across India through Satyajit Ray's 1974 film Sonar Kella ("The Golden Fortress"). Wisdom to carry forward Jaisalmer has survived nearly nine hundred years because people never stopped living in it. That is also why it is fragile. A museum fort only needs guarding. A living fort needs drains, water pipes and rubbish collection, as well as admiration for its carvings. The UNESCO decision about Jaisalmer is less about grand restoration than about plumbing. The ordinary infrastructure of daily life decides whether the extraordinary survives. Heritage is not only in the carved balconies. It is also in whether the water underneath them has somewhere to go. My connection We arrived in Jaisal

t: Shrinathji — When a Journey Became a Home
d: How a Krishna image from Govardhan found a new home in Mewar, and how devotion there gave rise to the art of Pichwai painting.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Shrinathji — When a Journey Became a Home Stories Behind the Stones Shrinathji — When a Journey Became a Home How a Krishna image from Govardhan found a new home in Mewar, and how devotion there gave rise to the art of Pichwai painting. Nathdwara Mewar Braj Vallabhacharya Maharana Raj Singh Vitthalnath Temples & Faith Art & Craft Legends & Folklore Sometimes, a place becomes famous not because a king founded a city, but because people believe the divine chose to stay there. Where and when The story of Nathdwara begins far away, at Govardhan Hill near Mathura. It begins in Braj, the Krishna country around Mathura in present-day Uttar Pradesh, and ends in Mewar, in southern Rajasthan, on the banks of the Banas river. Before Shrinathji came, the place was a village called Sihad (also written Sinhad). The temple is known as Shrinathji ki Haveli, the "mansion" of Shrinathji, and is run like a household. The people Shrinathji represents Lord Krishna as a young boy lifting Mount Govardhan to protect the people of Braj from torrential rain. His raised left arm recalls that beloved episode from Krishna's childhood. Shrinathji is especially important in the Pushtimarg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya, where devotion is expressed through loving service, known as seva. Vallabhacharya (usually dated 1479–1531) founded the Pushtimarg; Britannica records that he "discovered" the image at the foot of Govardhan. His son Vitthalnath is credited with shaping the elaborate daily seva that still structures worship of Shrinathji. Maharana Raj Singh of Mewar was the ruler who received the image in his kingdom. What happened During the seventeenth century, amid threats to temples in the Mathura region under Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, Shrinathji's image was moved from Govardhan in search of safety. In 1669–70 major temples were demolished on Aurangzeb's orders, including the Keshava Deva temple at Mathura. The temple's own account and museum catalogues agree that the image was moved to keep it safe. Historians still debate how far Aurangzeb's temple policy was driven by religion and how far by politics, and much of the detail of the journey comes to us through the community's own tradition. After a long journey, the image reached Mewar, where Maharana Raj Singh offered protection. Today, the temple is unlike many others. Shrinathji is cared for with the affection given to a beloved child. He is awakened, dressed, offered food and honoured through different darshans during the day. This devotion also gave rise to a remarkable artistic tradition. The beautiful painted cloth backdrops displayed behind Shrinathji are called Pichwai paintings. They portray lotuses, cows, peacocks, festivals, seasons and scenes from Krishna's life. Pichwais were changed daily, seasonally and for festivals: lotus ponds in summer, peacocks and dark clouds in the monsoon, brocades in winter. Families of painters settled in Nathdwara, and painters still work in the lane known as Chitron ki Gali, the street of paintings. For someone who loves traditional Indian painting, Nathdwara is therefore more than a pilgrimage destination. It is a place where devotion and art have grown together for centuries. Legends and debates And here comes the story that devotees continue to tell. As the cart carrying Shrinathji passed through the village of Sihad, its wheels became stuck in the ground. Despite repeated attempts, the cart would not move. The devotees interpreted this as a divine sign. Shrinathji had chosen his new home. A shrine was established there in 1672, and the settlement became known as Nathdwara — the gateway to the Lord. Which year? 1672 is the most commonly given date (the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the temple's own account), but the Victoria and Albert Museum gives 1671 and some sources give 1670. Wisdom to carry forward A home is not always the place where a journey begins. Sometimes, it is the place where one finally finds belonging. The journey of Shrinathji is remembered as a story of protection, faith and welcome. It also reminds us how one sacred tradition can shape an entire town — its art, music, food, festivals and everyday life. My connection We visited Shrinathji Temple at Nathdwara on the morning of 18 October, after leaving Kumbhalgarh at about 7:30, and before going on to Eklingji and Udaipur. In my diary I noted that the town is associated with Pichwai paintings, devotional works that depict Shrinathji and seasonal or festival settings, and that this connection between worship and painting naturally interested me. As I wrote then, "In Rajasthan, art so often belongs not only in galleries, but also in the rhythms of devotion." The next day in Udaipur I met artists who work in the miniature-painting tradition and learned about their processes, including how colours are prepared and how brushes are made. They were not Pichwai painters, but the conversation brought me closer to the kind of patient, inherited skill that this story is about. d: Saved as a baby, criticised as a king, Maharana Udai Singh II left Mewar something lasting: Udaipur, its new capital in the hills.
x: Home / Stories Behind the Stones / Udai Singh II and the City He Built Beside the Lake Stories Behind the Stones Udai Singh II and the City He Built Beside the Lake Saved as a baby, criticised as a king, Maharana Udai Singh II left Mewar something lasting: Udaipur, its new capital in the hills. Udaipur Chittorgarh Mewar Udai Singh II Panna Dhai Banbir Akbar Jaimal Rathore Patta Founders & Dynasties Forts & Palaces Legends & Folklore Udaipur, with its palaces rising from Lake Pichola, feels as if it was always meant to be there. In fact it was a new capital, created by a ruler of Mewar who was looking for somewhere safer than his ancestral fortress of Chittorgarh. That ruler was Maharana Udai Singh II, and history has not always been kind to him. His life began with one of Rajasthan's most famous rescue stories, and it ended in exile in the hills. In between, he made the decision that gave Mewar its future capital. Where and when In the early sixteenth century, Mewar's capital was the great hill fort of Chittorgarh. Udai Singh was born there on 4 August 1522 (the date given in standard accounts). He was a son of Rana Sanga, the famous Rajput king, and Rani Karnavati. After Sanga's death the kingdom went through years of turmoil: wars with Gujarat, a sack of Chittor in 1535, and murders within the royal family. The site he later chose for his new capital lay in the Girwa valley to the south-west. This is a fertile basin ringed by Aravalli hills. One history of the city notes that the surrounding terrain gave protection, because enemy cavalry and artillery could not move easily there. Lake Pichola already existed. It is believed to have been built in the fourteenth century, traditionally by a Banjara (trader) in 1362. The people Udai Singh II became Maharana after a dangerous childhood and ruled from the late 1530s until his death in 1572. Banbir was a relative who killed the reigning Rana, Vikramaditya (Udai Singh's half-brother), in the mid-1530s and seized power at Chittor. Panna Dhai was Udai Singh's nurse. In the traditional account, she saved his life (see below). Akbar , the Mughal emperor, besieged Chittorgarh in 1567–68. Jaimal Rathore of Badnore and Patta of Kelwa were the commanders Udai Singh left to defend Chittor. Maharana Pratap was Udai Singh's eldest son, who succeeded him. What happened According to the traditional account, when Banbir came to kill the young Udai Singh, his nurse Panna had him carried out of Chittor hidden in a basket, and laid her own son in the prince's bed. Banbir killed that child. Panna brought Udai Singh to Kumbhalgarh, where he was raised in secret. He was crowned there, in 1540 by most accounts, and later recovered Chittor from Banbir. As Maharana, Udai Singh began to develop the Girwa valley. The official Udaipur foundation history, published by the Maharana of Mewar Charitable Foundation, dates the founding of Udaipur to 1553. Other histories date the start of work to 1559, when the large lake named after him, Udai Sagar, was begun. Its dam is recorded as completed in 1565. The oldest part of the City Palace, the Rai Angan or royal courtyard, belongs to these early years. Later Maharanas kept adding to it for centuries. Then came the crisis. In October 1567 Akbar arrived outside Chittorgarh. On the advice of his council, Udai Singh withdrew to the hills of western Mewar and left the fort in the hands of Jaimal and Patta. The siege lasted about four months. Jaimal was killed by a musket shot, which Mughal sources say Akbar fired himself. On the night of 22 February 1568, Rajput women inside the fort committed jauhar , choosing death by fire rather than capture. The fort fell on 23 February 1568, and the historian Satish Chandra describes the killing of about 30,000 people, defenders and peasants who had taken refuge there. Chittor was lost, but Mewar was not conquered. Udai Singh held the western half of the kingdom. He died at Gogunda on 28 February 1572. His son Pratap would carry the resistance on, and Udaipur became the capital of Mewar. Legends and debates Panna Dhai. Her sacrifice is one of Rajasthan's best-known stories. James Tod's 1829 Annals describes her as a Khichi Rajput woman named Panna, "the Diamond", and says the boy was carried out by a bari (a servant) in a basket covered with leaves. Later retellings name her son Chandan. The story is told consistently in later chronicles and histories, but I have not found a contemporary record of the events. It is best read as tradition with a historical core. The hermit on the hill. The Mewar foundation history says that Udai Singh met a hermit, Goswami Prem Giri, on a hill above Pichola, who blessed him and told him to build his palace there. This is a founding legend. When was Udaipur founded? You will see 1553 (the Mewar foundation), 1559 (many histories, and Britannica's City Palace article) and 1568 (Britannica's entry on the city, which says Udaipur was made the capital that year, after Chittor fell). These dates need not conflict: building may have begun in the 1550s, while the city became the capital only after 1568. 1567 or 1568? The siege began in 1567 and the fort fell in 1568, so both years appear. Coward or strategist? Tod was scathing. He wrote that Udai Singh "had not one quality of a sovereign". Later writers often accused him of cowardice for leaving Chittor. The historian G. N. Sharma noted that he withdrew on his council's advice, and that no contemporary Persian author gave the impression of cowardice. Withdrawing to the hills was also exactly the strategy his son Pratap later used. Wisdom to carry forward The city I loved most on this journey exists because a king left a fortress instead of dying in it. For a long time that choice was told as a failure. Without it, there might have been no Udaipur and no base from which Mewar could continue. Retreat and defeat are not the same thing. x: Home / Travel Diaries / Rajasthan / Day 1 Part of My Rajasthan Diaries · Day 1 of 11 Day 1 — Jaipur: The Pink City Day 1, Saturday 10 October Jaipur: first impressions of the Pink City An ordinary airport, an extraordinary old city, and an artistic welcome. In this chapter Why “pink” when I see terracotta? Four landmarks, four different stories We began while Bengaluru was still asleep. Our flight left at 1:10 in the morning, and after a connection through Ahmedabad we reached Jaipur on the early morning flight. I had waited more than a decade to come to Rajasthan, so perhaps my expectations were unusually high. Even the airport, I imagined, might greet visitors with a hint of the state’s royal heritage. Instead it felt rather ordinary — and the heat was immediate. It was not quite the grand welcome I had pictured! We stayed at Arya Niwas, conveniently placed for exploring the old city. That choice worked beautifully: it was an economical, comfortable base, and we could reach the main sights without making every outing a major expedition. What caught my attention first, though, was not the convenience. It was the Mithila artwork on the walls. I practise and admire traditional Indian art, so seeing familiar motifs in a Jaipur hotel was an unexpected pleasure. One long painting, around five metres wide, was especially striking. Breakfast had another memorable detail: live sitar music. It was a lovely way to begin a day of sightseeing. Why “pink” when I see terracotta? After freshening up, we entered the old walled city. Suddenly the Jaipur I had imagined began to appear. Buildings stretched along the streets in a coordinated terracotta shade. Shop signs followed a similar visual pattern. Amid the bustle of traffic and commerce, there was an astonishing sense of uniformity. I kept looking from one building to the next, wondering how a living, busy city had retained such a distinct visual identity. I asked our guide a question that had been bothering me: why call it the Pink City when the colour looked terracotta? Jaipur’s buildings were famously painted for the 1876 visit of the Prince of Wales, later King Edward VII, with pink associated with hospitality. Our guide added an anecdote: that the visiting prince described the terracotta shade as pink and the description stayed. I enjoyed that explanation, although I treat that particular detail as the guide’s telling rather than a settled historical fact. Whatever the precise origin of the nickname, the city’s colour was unforgettable. Four landmarks, four different stories At City Palace we stepped into the history of Jaipur’s rulers and their taste for courtyards, ornament and ceremonial spaces. Jaipur itself was founded in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, and the city’s planned layout is part of what makes it remarkable. Its historic walled city is recognised by UNESCO. Jantar Mantar offered a very different kind of wonder. Here, enormous instruments of stone and masonry were built to observe the heavens and measure time. The site is a reminder that the ruler who founded Jaipur was deeply interested in astronomy. At Hawa Mahal, the honeycomb façade and rows of small windows showed another side of architecture: a building that is instantly recognisable, yet designed around climate, privacy and courtly life. Jal Mahal, appearing to float in Man Sagar Lake, gave us a quieter scene to look at. I liked all four places. Rather than selecting one as the winner, I enjoyed how different they were. By evening we had also seen the shops and markets of the Pink City. What stayed with me was not just the list of monuments, but the colour of the streets, the consistency of the signboards, the artwork at our hotel and the music over breakfast. Rajasthan was beginning to feel like a place where history and art could appear at any moment, even between the major attractions. The garden courtyard at Arya Niwas. City Palace: the Chandra Mahal courtyard and the museum’s silver thrones. Painted walls outside Raj Kala Mandir.
